memory_update.text: Use Vertiv as the high-attention reference leader for AI data-center power and thermal infrastructure; do not treat it as the underfollowed alpha candidate in later layers.

nVent should be tracked as a direct AI rack-level liquid-cooling and power-distribution supplier, especially around CDUs, manifolds, rear-door heat exchangers, smart PDUs, and data-center electrical connections.

Modine should be tracked as a thermal-management/data-center-cooling candidate where the key verification is data-center revenue mix and whether liquid cooling plus heat rejection becomes a durable growth segment.
Powell Industries is a second-order electrical balance-of-system candidate; survival into later layers depends on verifying data-center backlog repeatability rather than one-off project exposure.

Next Layer 1C/2 searches should add smaller component-level names in pumps, heat exchangers, cold plates, thermal interface materials, busways, backup power, commissioning, and electrical testing/inspection, because this pass stayed focused on direct public leaders and near-direct suppliers.
NVT should be stored as a reference comparator for data-center electrical and liquid-cooling infrastructure, not as the main underfollowed target.
MOD is a high-priority thermal-management candidate because its SEC filing directly links AI/HPC heat loads to hybrid and liquid-cooling demand and fiscal 2027 reporting should isolate Data Centers.
POWL is a power-distribution/switchgear candidate; the key Layer 2 task is verifying data-center order quality and whether backlog is recurring or project-lumpy.
ENS is a lower-attention reserve-power and UPS battery candidate; include in later screens only if data-center-specific Energy Systems growth can be quantified.
Need a separate pass for qualified installers and commissioning labor: IES Holdings and Comfort Systems USA appeared relevant, but were excluded due to the 4-candidate limit.
MOD should be tracked as an underfollowed data-center thermal-management candidate because Airedale has a disclosed multi-year strategic customer capacity agreement exceeding $4 billion through 2029.

POWL should be tracked as an electrical balance-of-system candidate for AI data centers, especially switchgear and packaged power systems, but exposure must be separated from utility, LNG, petrochemical, and other industrial backlog.

IESC should be tracked as a qualified-installer and data-center electrical/technology infrastructure execution candidate; key risk is whether high margins and backlog are sustainable or project-lumpy.
NVT and AAON have strong node evidence and should be reviewed in a follow-up pass, but were excluded from the 4-name cap to preserve one reference anchor plus three underfollowed names.

For this node, the next filter should quantify actual data-center revenue/backlog share, capacity expansion, lead times, customer concentration, and margin durability rather than relying on generic AI-infrastructure labels.
AAON should be tracked as an HVAC-labeled but increasingly data-center-cooling-exposed name; key evidence is BASX sales, backlog growth, liquid-cooling mix, and data-center customer durability.
POWL maps to the electrical distribution/switchgear chokepoint; the USD 400M-plus data-center order is strong evidence, but the thesis must be tested for lumpiness and repeatability.
IESC maps to the qualified installer/custom infrastructure solutions lane; it is a second-order AI beneficiary where the bottleneck may be field execution capacity rather than proprietary components.
nVent and Atkore are strong near-miss candidates for a follow-up pass focused specifically on racks, CDUs, manifolds, intelligent PDUs, cable pathway, and electrical balance-of-system components.

For this node, market mapping should separate four sub-bottlenecks: integrated power/thermal platforms, specialized cooling equipment, medium-voltage/switchgear systems, and qualified electrical/MEP installation capacity.
